entries.title: Indoor infrared saunas compared
entries.description: Indoor infrared saunas from Peak, JNH and others compared by size, seats, power and the circuit they need.
entries.heading: Indoor infrared saunas compared
introduction: These infrared cabins are made for indoor use. Most run on 120 volts, but the circuit behind the outlet differs a lot, from 10 amps up to 30.
The order says nothing about quality. We compare specs and haven't sat in any of these.

sections.heading: Measure more than the cabin
paragraphs: The sizes in the table are the cabin's outside dimensions. You also need room for the door to open and the gaps the manual asks for. Most makers don't publish those clearances on the product page, so look in the installation manual before you pick a corner.

sections.heading: Same voltage, different circuits
paragraphs: Peak lists 10 amps for the Mini, 15 for the Crown and Shasta, and a dedicated 20-amp circuit for the Everest and Fuji. JNH says a standard 15-amp outlet is enough for its one- and two-person Tosi, while the Tosi Red for four needs its own 20-amp line.
So a 120-volt plug doesn't mean any outlet will do. Check the breaker, see what else is on it, and ask an electrician if you're unsure.

entries.title: JNH Lifestyles saunas
entries.description: The JNH Lifestyles Tosi and Arki saunas: sizes from one to four people, power and circuits compared.
entries.heading: JNH Lifestyles saunas
introduction: We list four JNH saunas. The Tosi comes for one, two or four people and stays indoors. The Arki Outdoor Duo is the one for outside and seats two.

sections.heading: Sizes
paragraphs: The Tosi 1-Person is 35.5 inches wide, the 2-Person 47.3 and the Red 4-Person 70.9. The Arki is its own design and not an outdoor version of the Tosi.

sections.heading: Power
paragraphs: All four run on 120 volts. JNH says a standard 15-amp outlet is fine for the one- and two-person Tosi. The Tosi Red and the Arki each need a dedicated 20-amp circuit.

entries.title: Infrared sauna electrical requirements
entries.description: Why a 120-volt infrared sauna may still need its own 20- or 30-amp circuit, with examples from Peak, JNH and others.
entries.heading: What electrical hookup does an infrared sauna need?
introduction: Most infrared saunas run on 120 volts, the same as any outlet in the house. What differs is the current. Small ones are happy on a 15-amp circuit, bigger ones want 20 or 30 amps to themselves.

sections.heading: What to look for in the specs
paragraphs: Look for four things: volts, amps, plug type and the words "dedicated circuit". A NEMA 5-15 plug fits a normal outlet. A 5-20 has one blade turned sideways and needs a 20-amp receptacle. Dedicated means nothing else shares the breaker.
Use the numbers for the exact size you're buying. The four-person version of a sauna often needs a bigger circuit than the two-person one.

sections.heading: When the maker doesn't say
paragraphs: Peak lists 120 volts for the Mini and Crown but no circuit size. JNH is clearer: a standard 110-volt, 15-amp outlet is enough for its one- and two-person Tosi models.
If the circuit isn't stated, ask the seller in writing and show the answer to your electrician. Skip adapters and extension cords.

entries.title: 2-Person Home Saunas: Size, Power and Wiring
entries.description: 2-person home saunas compared by size, voltage and power: 120-volt infrared cabins and 240-volt traditional saunas.
entries.heading: 2-person saunas compared
introduction: Two seats is the most common size on our list, and the choice comes down to two kinds. Infrared cabins draw roughly 1.5 to 3.4 kW and mostly run on 120 volts. Traditional saunas have a 4.5 to 8 kW heater and, where the maker says, need 220 or 240 volts on a 30- or 40-amp circuit.

sections.heading: How much room they take
paragraphs: The smallest is the JNH Tosi 2-Person at 47.3 by 39.5 inches. The Peak Crown, Everest and Fuji are 48 to 53 inches wide and 44 deep. Traditional cabins are bigger because the heater and its guard take up bench space: the Salus Ally is 60 by 46 inches, the Almost Heaven Hillsboro 63 by about 45 and the Sweat Kingdom Sweat Pod 53 by 61.
Add the clearances from the manual and room for the door.

sections.heading: Power and running cost
paragraphs: Infrared models here are rated from 1,540 to 3,350 watts. Traditional ones start at 4,500 and go up to 8,000 for the Sweat Kingdom Summit. You'll notice that in the wiring and on the bill.
A traditional heater runs flat out while it warms up and then cycles on and off. The running cost guide has dollar figures for every state.
points: Infrared, 120 volts: JNH Tosi 2-Person, JNH Arki Outdoor Duo, Peak Crown, Peak Everest, Peak Fuji, Sun Home Eclipse 2
Traditional, 220 or 240 volts or not stated: Almost Heaven, Finnleo, Salus, SunRay and Sweat Kingdom

sections.heading: Check the breaker too
paragraphs: Even among 120-volt models, the circuit differs. The Tosi 2-Person works on 15 amps, the Everest, Fuji and Arki Outdoor Duo need 20, and the Sun Home Eclipse 2 draws 23.5 amps and needs a 30-amp circuit.
Several Sweat Kingdom models list power and amps but no voltage. Ask before ordering.

entries.title: 120V plug-in saunas compared
entries.description: Saunas that plug into 120 volts: all of them infrared, from one to four seats, needing circuits from 15 to 30 amps.
entries.heading: 120-volt plug-in saunas
introduction: If you want a sauna without running a 240-volt line, you're looking at infrared. Every 120-volt model we list is an infrared cabin, rated between 1.2 and 2.8 kW. Some of them still need their own circuit.

sections.heading: Why no traditional ones?
paragraphs: The smallest traditional heater on our list is 4,000 watts, the typical one 6,000. On 120 volts that would pull 33 to 50 amps, far too much for a household circuit. If you want a stove and steam, plan for 240 volts.

sections.heading: Circuits from 15 to 30 amps
paragraphs: The Peak Mini draws 10 amps. The JNH Tosi for one and two, Peak Rainier and Peak Shasta are made for 15-amp circuits. The Peak Everest and Fuji, JNH Tosi Red 4-Person, JNH Arki Outdoor Duo and Sun Home Equinox need 20. The Sun Home Eclipse 2 draws 23.5 amps and needs 30, even though it runs on 120 volts.
The number is printed on your breaker. Whether the wiring and outlet match is a question for an electrician.

sections.heading: Sizes
paragraphs: One-person cabins start at 31 by 32 inches (Peak Mini) and go up to 42 by 40 (Rainier and Shasta). Two-person models are 47 to 55 inches wide. The Sun Home Equinox seats three, the JNH Tosi Red four at 70.9 by 47.3 inches. Only the Arki Outdoor Duo is made for outdoors.

entries.title: What does it cost to run a sauna?
entries.description: Cost per hour for infrared and traditional saunas, calculated with 2026 home electricity prices for all 50 states and DC.
entries.heading: What does it cost to run a home sauna?
introduction: About 37 cents an hour for a typical infrared cabin and about $1.09 for a traditional sauna, at the 2026 US average of 18.19 cents per kWh. Your state changes that by a factor of almost four.

sections.heading: How we calculated it
paragraphs: Power times price. We take the rated power of each model and the average home electricity price for January to July 2026 from the Energy Information Administration. Models without a stated power are left out.
The result is the cost at full power. A traditional heater only runs flat out while it heats up, so an actual hour is usually cheaper.

sections.heading: Per session
paragraphs: Count the warm-up. Heat a 6 kW sauna for 45 minutes, use it for 30, and you pay $1.36 at most. Forty minutes in a 2.05 kW infrared cabin stays under 25 cents.

sections.heading: Your state matters most
paragraphs: North Dakota paid 12.36 cents per kWh, California 33.25 and Hawaii 46.28. The same 6 kW heater costs $0.74, $2.00 or $2.78 an hour. Your own rate is on your bill, so use that if you want it exact.
